decision: Set the exit condition as: every service serves its step commands on one durable consumer, the gates pass, and a fresh provision plus an ORE import run end to end.
why: A run this long needs a checkable predicate instead of a feeling

decision: Probed the live 2.14.6 server: a durable consumer accepts a filter-set change in place and keeps its cursor.
why: Decides whether reconciling a consumer must delete it (losing its position and replaying the backlog) or can update it
evidence: nats probe on ores_dev_brave_hopper_dsh_probe, deleted after
result: filter set widened from 1 to 3 filters, delivered seq stayed 3

decision: Confined the replay hazard: refdata_steps currently holds 184 retained commands, so a new consumer name would replay them.
why: Makes the upgrade path a real risk rather than a guess

decision: Reconciled a durable by updating its stored config in place instead of deleting it, so the consumer keeps its position.
why: Deleting it replayed a day of step commands on a filter change; refdata_steps alone holds 184.

decision: Declared one step_routes table per family and derived the stream, the consumer filters and the dispatch from it.
why: One consumer per subject is what left orphans and name collisions; one list cannot disagree with itself.

decision: Probed the live server again: limits retention can be changed to interest in place, keeping max age.
why: Decides whether the retention backstop can migrate an existing stream or needs a recreate.
evidence: nats probe on ores_dev_brave_hopper_dsh_probe4, deleted after

decision: Moved the ack guard out of the twelve registrar lambdas and into the handler methods, so a path that records no outcome is retried instead of accepted.
why: The lambda accepted after the handler returned, whether or not the handler had recorded anything.

decision: Added jetstream_admin::prune_consumers and call it after subscribe, so a service deletes the consumers it no longer declares.
why: The old per-subject consumers hold no work once one consumer filters the whole family, and under interest retention they would pin messages.

decision: Set the step streams to interest retention with a one-day backstop, and made ensure_stream reconcile the retention and the age in place.
why: A command stream should not accumulate a day of every step; the server accepts the policy change live, verified by probe.

decision: Wrote the At Least Once Prerequisites pattern page and refreshed the JetStream architecture page to the new stream, consumer and retention contract.
why: The library states the target state; the architecture page is the catalogue, so both had to move with the code.

decision: Gave the reporting, ore, identity, compute and refdata rewiring to two children with a written recipe, then reviewed their diffs and judged every early return by reading the artifacts.
why: Twelve registrars and thirteen handlers is more edits than one context should hold; the recipe is the lever they all read.
result: both reported; build proof is mine

decision: Captured the consumer shape of all 15 step streams before the deploy, as the before side of the comparison.
why: A check that only runs after the change cannot show the change; the script is rerunnable on the real server.
result: FAIL: 15 of 15 streams, 88 consumers in total, none named after its stream

decision: Syntax-checked the 21 changed translation units with the build's own flags while the locked full build was still running.
why: The full build serialises on a worktree lock and takes hours under load; the changed set is small and known.

decision: Restarted the fleet onto the new binaries. Every step stream now carries exactly one consumer named after it, on interest retention, with a one-day age limit.
why: This is the upgrade test: the live streams still held 88 per-subject consumers from the old code.
result: PASS 15 of 15 streams; 24 services running, 0 failed

decision: Planted a consumer named dsh-dummy on assets_steps, restarted the service, and confirmed it was deleted with the prune log line.
why: The outcome alone could hide a prune that never ran, so the mechanism needed its own experiment.

decision: The prune log accounts for 59 of the 88 baseline consumers. The other 29 were already absent when the new code first ran, so prune found nothing to delete.
why: Nine streams had no prune line yet hold exactly one consumer now. I could not establish what removed those 29 earlier, and the stream creation times rule out a stream recreate.

decision: Recreated the database and provisioned ACME on the rebuilt services. Every workflow the provision started reached a terminal state.
why: This is the real end-to-end check: the provision dispatches data-quality step commands to a dozen services.
result: 23 bundle_publish + 1 provision_tenant + 1 tenant_setup, all completed, 0 non-terminal steps

decision: Verified the consumer shape again on the freshly created streams, after the purge removed every stream.
why: The first check exercised the update path on streams that already existed; this one exercises the create path.
result: PASS 15 of 15, retention interest, max_age 1 day

decision: Triggered a report instance. The run walked its whole forward path and then its compensations, across three services, and reached a terminal state.
why: A report run is the only path that exercises the reporting execution, ore and compute step families in one go.
result: report_execution_workflow compensated: steps 0-4 completed, step 5 failed on an authz refusal

decision: Traced the one failed step to a forbidden response from compute.v1.workunits.list_by_batch_id, which the compute registrar serves with queue_subscribe on core NATS.
why: The refusal must not be mistaken for a step-delivery defect; the step command itself was delivered and answered.
result: unrelated to this change; all 78 report definitions use post_processing execute, so no definition can pass it here

decision: Ran ctest for the nats, service, workflow, reporting, compute and refdata components.
why: The change touches a header almost every service includes, so the components it touches needed their own suites run.

decision: Ran the repo gate set. Fixed the two failures this branch caused; two others pre-date it.
why: A clean compile is not a gate pass, and a gate failure needs a cause before it needs a fix.
result: 50 of 52 pass; component-drift and cmake-sources fail in components and files this branch does not touch

decision: Ended the dispatch log chain on a literal, which keeps the subject conformance scanner's regex from reading the line's own label as a declared subject.
why: The scanner matches subject= inside string literals; removing the trailing literal exposed a match that ran to a later apostrophe.

decision: Re-ran the whole static gate set after fixing all four failures.
why: The first run left four red; three were reachable from this branch and one was pre-existing drift in components it touches.

decision: Registered the step command stream header in its component list and regenerated the two handlers the template had drifted from.
why: Both were omissions from earlier work on this branch, not of the gate's making.

decision: Re-ran the prune experiment and saved the transcript, so the claim rests on an artifact rather than on a journal grep run by hand.
why: A row whose evidence is a command someone had to be present to watch is not reviewable after the fact.
result: PASS: dsh-dummy3 planted, gone after the restart, prune logged

decision: Accounted for the one replay the rename can cause: a new consumer name starts at the stream's oldest retained command, and the backlog was already purged because the retention change drops every acknowledged command before the new consumer exists.
why: The upgrade had to be shown safe, not assumed safe, because refdata_steps alone held 184 retained commands before the restart.
evidence: journalctl 'Serving 47 step command(s)' and 'Pruned 50 consumer(s)'; stream info shows refdata_steps at 0 messages after the restart
result: no replay observed; the work is also repeat-safe because the publish steps are upserts and the engine ignores a completion for a step no longer in progress
